criteria.descriptor: Full marks: correctly describes the semantic-cache mechanism, accurately distinguishes it from prompt/prefix (KV) caching (lossless prefix/KV reuse reducing prefill/TTFT vs approximate model-skipping), and states technically sound failure modes and fixes (false hits, staleness/embedding-model invalidation, cross-user leakage). Deduct for conflating the two caching types, calling semantic caching lossless, or asserting incorrect mechanics.

Full marks: covers the mechanism/benefit, the prefix-caching contrast, all three main risk classes (false hits, staleness/invalidation, personalization/multi-tenancy), concrete safeguards, and a metrics/measurement plan. Partial credit as classes are omitted.

Full marks: justifies choices with mechanisms -- why a fixed cosine threshold is a precision/recall trade-off, why prefix and semantic caching are complementary, why the cache key must be partitioned -- rather than asserting fixes. Deduct when recommendations are stated without a why or without acknowledging the trade-off.

Full marks: a well-organised critique that separates the contrast, the risks, and the safeguards/metrics, uses correct vocabulary (TTFT, prefill/KV, ANN, false-hit rate, invalidation), and stays within the length. Deduct for disorganised or vague phrasing.

expected_answer_points: Explains the semantic-cache mechanism (embed query, ANN lookup, serve stored answer above a similarity threshold) and its benefit -- serves paraphrases and skips the full retrieval+generation call, cutting cost and latency -- versus exact-match caching

Correctly contrasts prompt/prefix (KV) caching as lossless reuse of computed KV states for a shared exact prefix that reduces prefill/TTFT and input cost but still decodes every request, against semantic caching which skips the model entirely and is approximate/lossy; notes they are complementary

Identifies the false-hit risk: embeddings can be close for queries with opposite intent, negation, or different entities/numbers, so a single fixed threshold returns confidently wrong answers (precision/recall trade-off)

Identifies staleness/invalidation: cached answers go stale when the knowledge base changes, and changing the embedding model invalidates stored vectors; requires TTL plus version/event-based invalidation

Identifies personalization/multi-tenant/privacy risk: caching across users can leak PII or return wrong per-user answers, so the cache key must include user/tenant/locale/KB-version context and only non-personalized queries should be cached
Proposes concrete safeguards: empirically validated threshold, secondary verification for borderline hits, fallback to the full pipeline on low confidence, and scoping what is cacheable
Names the right metrics: hit rate AND a correctness/false-hit guardrail (sample and grade cached responses), cost/latency savings, and hit-vs-miss latency -- not hit rate alone
common_pitfalls: Conflates semantic caching with prompt/prefix (KV) caching -- treating both as the same mechanism or claiming semantic caching is lossless like prefix caching
Endorses the design on hit rate and cost savings alone, never recognising the false-hit correctness risk of returning a semantically-near but wrong cached answer
Assumes a single global cache is fine, missing multi-tenant/personalization: PII leakage and per-user-context correctness (cache key needs tenant/user/locale/KB-version)
Forgets staleness -- that a knowledge-base update or a change of embedding model invalidates cached entries -- so proposes no TTL or invalidation
Offers only 'raise the threshold' with no empirical validation, secondary check, or fallback, or picks a threshold with no measurement basis
Proposes caching everything, including account-specific or action/tool-invoking queries that must never be served from a stale approximate cache
reference_answer:
Semantic caching is attractive because, unlike exact-match caching, it can serve paraphrases of previously answered questions and skips the entire retrieval+generation pipeline, cutting both cost and latency for the matched requests. But it is fundamentally lossy/approximate, and that is where the risks live.

Contrast with prompt/prefix (KV) caching: provider or server-side prefix caching (Anthropic prompt caching, OpenAI/vLLM automatic prefix caching) reuses the computed attention key/value states for a shared exact prompt prefix -- typically the system prompt, few-shot examples, or long retrieved context -- so the prefill step is not recomputed. It is lossless (same output distribution), still runs decoding for every request, and mainly reduces TTFT and input-token cost. Semantic caching instead skips the model call entirely and returns a stored response, so it is approximate and can be wrong. The two are complementary: use prefix caching to make the calls you still make cheaper, and semantic caching to avoid some calls.

Main failure modes of the proposal: (1) False hits -- embeddings can be near for queries with opposite intent or different critical entities/numbers/negation ('cancel order 123' vs '456', 'how to enable' vs 'disable'), so a single fixed cosine threshold returns confidently wrong answers; threshold is a precision/recall trade-off. (2) Staleness -- when the knowledge base changes (policies, prices) cached answers go stale; changing the embedding model invalidates all stored vectors. (3) Personalization/multi-tenant leakage -- answers that depend on user, account state, permissions, or locale can leak PII or be wrong if cached across users.

Safe deployment: only cache generic, non-personalized, stable queries (never account-specific or action/tool queries); make the cache key = embedding plus explicit partition filters (tenant, locale, KB version, embedding-model version); choose the threshold empirically on a labeled set and add a cheap secondary check (cross-encoder or lightweight LLM verify) for borderline hits; fall through to the full pipeline on low confidence; apply TTL plus event-based invalidation on KB updates. Measure not just hit rate and cost/latency savings, but a quality guardrail -- sample cached-served answers and grade correctness (false-hit rate) -- and track hit vs miss latency separately.
